EXPLAIN THE SOLUTION TO THE JURY

Optimality you can verify

01

Measured terrain

Measured DTM elevations → native slopes. Each route node retains the maximum slope of its source cells; image resolution and route spacing are reported separately. Missing data and slopes above the limit are excluded.

02

The cost of every step

Rolling + ascent + auxiliary power and heating in transit. Slopes increase travel time. Stop energy and the return trip are included before checking reserves.

03

Search and constraints

A* minimizes energy on an 8-neighbour graph without cutting blocked corners. If the energy minimum exceeds the time budget, the search retains nondominated energy/time pairs.

04

Verify the result

The standard result is checked against Dijkstra. With an active time constraint, A* finishes only when no remaining lower bound can improve on the solution.

Model formula and scope of the claim

E = Σ [m · 3.71 · Crr · d / η + m · 3.71 · max(Δh, 0) / η] / 3 600 000 + P · t / 1000

E is in kWh, d is horizontal distance in metres, P is in watts and t is in hours. Edge time: √(d²+Δh²) / v × [1 + 2(slope / limit)²]. This is a configurable engineering model, not a measured relationship for a specific rover. On the return trip, positive ascent changes direction.

“Optimal” means the lowest model energy among feasible paths on the selected finite graph with the specified endpoints, area boundary, resources and same-path return constraint. It is neither a global optimum on the continuous Martian surface nor a survival probability.

An operational mission requires local stereo cameras, soil bearing-capacity data, rock detection, validated drivetrain and life-support models, communications, radiation and weather information. Grid spacing does not guarantee detection of every wheel-scale obstacle.
